purpose: Proposed whole-course outline for Claude; not a canonical route, design or coverage approval
identifierPolicy: Exact CMS codenames; retain sourceHtml (crosswalk) for official mathematical layout

idPrefixMapping.note: Algebraic techniques first, then functions, lines, quadratics, other graphs and properties.
One numbering across both trigonometry focus areas; each video records its own focus area.
c for calculus, as the brief suggests. Year 12 keeps d for its differential calculus.
g is free in the Year 11 namespace (Year 12 uses math-a12-g for practice). Year 11 practice uses p.

recommendedStrandOrder: Probability and data (s01-s11), can run in parallel at any point
orderReasons: Working with functions comes first: index laws, factorising, surds, quadratics, function notation, domain and line equations are used by every later strand.

Differentiation comes next because it needs only functions, lines (tangents and normals) and index laws, and because the Year 12 videos already designed and built (math-a12-d01 onward) assume Year 11 differentiation. The Year 11 videos they lean on (c07, c10, e01, e02) should exist early.
Exponentials and logarithms follow differentiation because the 2024 syllabus defines e through the gradient of y = a^x at x = 0, which needs tangent gradients (c04 to c07).

Trigonometry is self-contained after Stage 5 and functions. Year 12 trig derivatives (d05) and trig transformations (t01 to t03) need it, so it must precede those in the playlist, but not the calculus strands.
Graph transformations need the graphs they act on: parabolas, cubics, hyperbolas, absolute value, circles, exponentials and logs. Year 12 t01 then extends the same principles to trig graphs.
Probability and data has no calculus or trig prerequisite and can be produced in parallel. Year 12 random variables need it.

The 2024 syllabus lists the focus areas in the order functions, trig measure, trig identities, differentiation, exponentials, transformations, probability. That listing is not a mandated teaching order; this order follows prerequisites and the existing Year 12 dependencies.

d01.text: Conclude that Euler’s number, e, is a unique number such that d/dx (e^x) = e^x, that is, e^x is its own derivative

Apply the fact that the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives: d/dx (f(x) + g(x)) = f'(x) + g'(x), and the derivative of a multiple of a function is the multiple of its derivative: d/dx (k ⋅ f(x)) = k ⋅ f'(x)
Graph the exponential functions y = k(a^x) and y = k(a^(-x)) for constants a and k where a > 0, a ≠ 1 and k ≠ 0, and identify its asymptote, y-intercept, domain and range

Use the notation d/dx (f(x)) and f'(x) for the derivative of a function f(x)
Use the formula d/dx (x^n) = nx^(n - 1) for all real values of n

Apply the fact that the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives: d/dx (f(x) + g(x)) = f'(x) + g'(x), and the derivative of a multiple of a function is the multiple of its derivative: d/dx (k ⋅ f(x)) = k ⋅ f'(x)
Use the rules for differentiation to find equations of tangents and normals to a curve at points on the curve
Find points on a curve where the tangent or normal has a given gradient

Examine and use the relationship between the angle of inclination of a line or tangent to a curve, θ, with the positive x-axis, and the gradient, m, of that line or tangent, and establish that tan θ = m

Apply the product rule: if y = uv, where u and v are both differentiable functions of x, then dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx or if h(x) = f(x)g(x) for differentiable functions f(x) and g(x) then h'(x) = f(x)g'(x) + f'(x)g(x)

Apply the quotient rule: if y = u/v, where u and v are both differentiable functions of x, then dy/dx = (v du/dx - u dv/dx)/(v^2) or if h(x) = (f(x))/(g(x)) then h'(x) = (g(x)f'(x) - f(x)g'(x))/([g(x)]^2)

Apply the chain rule: if y is a differentiable function of u, and u is a differentiable function of x, then dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx or if h(x) = f(g(x)) for differentiable functions f(x) and g(x) then h'(x) = f'(g(x))g'(x)
Identify and apply the product, quotient or chain rule, or a combination of the rules, as appropriate to differentiate a given function
Interpret f(x) as increasing at x = c when f'(c) > 0 and decreasing at x = c when f'(c) < 0
Describe the behaviour of a function at a point as stationary when the tangent at the point is parallel to the x-axis, and recognise that f(x) is stationary at x = c when f'(c) = 0
Graph y = f'(x) for a given graph of a function y = f(x)
Numerically estimate the value of the derivative at a point on the graph of a power of x, with and without the use of digital tools
Identify stationary points on the graph of a cubic function, and the values of x for which the function is increasing and/or decreasing, by first calculating the derivative, and justify conclusions

sourcePoints.group: The derivative as a rate of change
sourcePoints.text: Interpret f'(c) as the instantaneous rate of change of the function f(x) at x = c

sourcePoints.group: The derivative as a rate of change
sourcePoints.text: Define and distinguish between displacement and distance and between velocity and speed

sourcePoints.group: The derivative as a rate of change
sourcePoints.text: Use graphs of functions and their derivatives, without the use of algebraic techniques, to describe and interpret physical phenomena

sourcePoints.group: The derivative as a rate of change
sourcePoints.text: Use the notation dx/dt or ẋ to represent the velocity of a particle with displacement x from a point as a function of time t

sourcePoints.group: The derivative as a rate of change
sourcePoints.text: Solve problems by determining the velocity of a particle moving in a straight line, given its displacement from a point as a function of time
Graph the exponential functions y = k(a^x) and y = k(a^(-x)) for constants a and k where a > 0, a ≠ 1 and k ≠ 0, and identify its asymptote, y-intercept, domain and range
Describe the behaviour of y = k(a^x) and y = k(a^(-x)) as x → ∞ and x → -∞

Examine the gradient of the tangent to the curve y = a^x at its y-intercept for varying values of a, and verify using graphing applications that there is a unique number e ≈ 2.71828182845..., such that the gradient of the tangent to y = e^x at x = 0 is 1, and call this number e Euler’s number
Examine the gradient function of y = a^x with graphing applications and identify that the gradient function is d/dx (a^x) = ka^x, for some constant k depending only on a
Conclude that Euler’s number, e, is a unique number such that d/dx (e^x) = e^x, that is, e^x is its own derivative
Define the logarithm of a number y, where y > 0, to any positive base a as the index to which a is raised to give y
Use the notation log_a y for the logarithm of y to the base a
Define the natural logarithm ln a = log_e a
Use digital tools to determine rational and irrational values of exponential and logarithmic expressions
Explain that y = a^x is equivalent to x = log_a y for a > 0 and a ≠ 1, and use the equivalence to solve equations of the form a^x = b, for a > 0
Recognise and use the logarithmic properties: log_a a^x = x for all real x, a^(log_a x) = x where x > 0
Derive the laws of logarithms from the laws of indices log_a m + log_a n = log_a (mn), log_a m - log_a n = log_a (m/n) and log_a (m^n) = nlog_a m
Justify the logarithmic results log_a a = 1, log_a 1 = 0 and log_a (1/x) = -log_a x
Apply the logarithmic laws and results to simplify expressions, solve equations and prove results, using digital tools where necessary
Prove the change of base rule log_a x = (log_b x)/(log_b a) and use it to solve problems
Graph the logarithmic function y = log_a x for a > 0 and a ≠ 1
Use graphing applications to identify the graphs of y = a^x and y = log_a x as reflections of each other in the line y = x, in cases where a > 1 and 0 < a < 1

Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by -x in the equation of a graph corresponds to the reflection of the graph in the y-axis, and that replacing y by -y corresponds to a reflection in the x-axis

Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by x - a in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal translation of a graph by a, that replacing y by y - b corresponds to a vertical translation by b, and recognise that the sign of a and b determines the direction of the translation
Describe a horizontal dilation as a stretch from the y-axis and a vertical dilation as a stretch from the x-axis

Establish using graphing applications that replacing x by x/k in the equation of a graph corresponds to a horizontal dilation of a graph by a factor of k, that replacing y by y/l corresponds to a vertical dilation by a factor of l, and determine the effects on the graph when the magnitude of the dilation factor lies between 0 and 1

Establish, using graphing applications, replacing x by x/k and replacing y by y/k in the equation of a graph corresponds to a dilation by a factor of k, that is, an enlargement of the graph when k > 1 and a reduction of the graph when 0 < k < 1

Apply reflections, translations and dilations to functions within the scope of the Mathematics Advanced course, excluding trigonometric functions, determine the function rule and the graph of the transformed function, the domain and range of the transformed graph, any intercepts, asymptotes and discontinuities where appropriate, and describe which transformations have been applied
Use the principles of translations to identify the centre, radius, domain and range of graphs of circles in the form (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2, where a, b and r are constants
Find the centre and radius of circles of the form x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0, where a, b and c are constants, by completing the squares
Graph circles given their equations and find the equation of a circle from its graph
Recognise that the order in which individual transformations are applied to functions is important
Define a set as a collection of objects, called the elements of the set, and represent a set using notation such as {2,3,5,7} and {0,2,4,6, …}
Use the notation n(A) or |A| to represent the number of elements in a finite set A
Define the empty set as the set with no elements, denoted in set notation as ∅
Use the notation A̅, A' or A^c to represent the complement of a set A with respect to some universal set U
Define A to be a subset of B if all the elements of A are elements of B
Define the intersection A ∩ B of sets A and B to be the set of elements that are in A and in B
Define the union A ∪ B of sets A and B to be the set of elements that are in A or in B
Define sets A and B to be disjoint if A ∩ B = ∅, that is, they have no elements in common
Use Venn diagrams in practical situations to represent and interpret sets that may intersect in various ways within a universal set
Establish and use the rule |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|
Define an experiment or a trial to be any procedure that can be infinitely repeated and has a well-defined set of possible outcomes known as the sample space, denoted S
Identify an event A as a subset A of the sample space S
Define the probability of each outcome to be 1/(|S|) when all the outcomes are equally likely and the probability of the event A to be P(A) = (|A|)/(|S|)
Interpret the notation A̅ to be the event ‘ A does not occur’, interpret A ∩ B to be the event ‘ A and B both occur’, and interpret A ∪ B to be the event ‘ A or B occurs’
Use Venn diagrams to represent the relationship between events within the same sample space, including mutually exclusive events, that is, events that as subsets of the sample space are disjoint
Establish and use the rules P(A̅) = 1 - P(A) and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)
Use arrays and tree diagrams to determine the outcomes and probabilities for multistage events
Define conditional probability as the probability that an event A occurs given that another event B has already occurred, and use the notation P(A|B)
Examine conditional probability by restricting the sample space and event spaces in a Venn diagram, using a two-way table, a tree diagram and other arrays
Establish that P(A|B) = (|A ∩ B|)/(|B|) when all outcomes are equally likely by restricting the sample space and event space, and hence P(A|B) = (P(A ∩ B))/(P(B)), provided |B| ≠ 0
Use the formulas for P(A|B) to solve practical problems involving conditional probability
Define two events to be independent if the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability that the other event occurs
Explain that two events A and B are independent means P(A|B) = P(A) and P(B|A) = P(B), and show algebraically that if one of these formulas is true, then the other is also true

Use the formula P(A|B) = (P(A ∩ B))/(P(B)), and the test P(A|B) = P(A) for independence to prove that if two events are independent, then P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), and to prove conversely that if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), then A and B are independent
Solve practical problems involving independent events
Define a random variable as a variable whose value is the outcome of a random experiment
Compare discrete random variables with continuous random variables, describe their differences, and give practical examples of each
Organise finite datasets using a table or a spreadsheet, listing the values, frequency, relative frequency, cumulative frequency, and cumulative relative frequency

Graph the frequency, relative frequency, and cumulative frequency histograms and polygons of datasets, using spreadsheets or graphing applications, and identify the mode and median from the graphs, and from tables
Use the relative frequency to estimate the probability of results in experiments

siteMissingOrPartial.gap: A relation is defined as a set of ordered pairs and an input-output mapping. The idea of an association between the elements of two sets is not shown explicitly (no two-set arrow picture).
x-intercepts as zeros are taught for parabolas. The general statement that the y-intercept is f(0) appears only as a fixed-fee remark in WF02.

Simultaneous linear equations appear inside break-even and intersection work. A general practical pair-of-lines problem solved both algebraically and graphically, with and without a graphing application, is not worked as its own task.
Only y = kx (n = 1) is taught. The syllabus model is y = kx^n.
Only y = k/x (n = 1) is taught. The syllabus model is y = k/x^n.
Finding k from one pair is taught for n = 1 only.
Graphing and domain/range of piecewise functions are taught. Testing a piecewise function for even or odd symmetry is not.
No lesson shows by numerical substitution that the square root of x squared equals |x|.
Graphs of y = |ax + b| with symmetry, domain and range are not developed as a set task; GT06, which graphs absolute value transformations, is retired as Extension 1 content.
Solved algebraically (ax + b = c or ax + b = -c). The graphical solution (intersection with y = k) is not taught.
Coterminal angles and the terminal side are named, but the idea that one ray represents infinitely many angles is not developed in degrees on the Cartesian plane.
Only the unit circle (r = 1) is used. The definitions cos = x/r, sin = y/r, tan = y/x on a circle of radius r are not developed.
Values at multiples of 90 degrees and undefined tan are given in the domain-and-range lesson, not evaluated from the x/r, y/r, y/x definitions.
cos(-x) = cos x and tan(-x) = -tan x appear as even/odd graph facts. The three results are not established together from the circle definitions.
Reciprocal functions are defined as 1/sin, 1/cos, 1/tan. They are not defined first as side ratios (hypotenuse/adjacent and so on) for acute angles.
No lesson justifies sec, cosec and cot at 0 and 90 degrees by letting a right-angled triangle tend to those angles.
The definitions sec = r/x, cosec = r/y, cot = x/y on a circle of radius r are not developed.
The gradient of a linear model as its rate is taught in WF18. The differentiation lessons do not connect a constant rate to the linear case.
ID13 builds the secant table for x squared only. The pattern nx^(n-1) is stated as a rule in ID04 rather than inferred from several powers and verified with a graphing application.
The tangent-gradient definition is given, but the condition that the tangent must exist and not be vertical is not stated.
One practical graph (a draining tank) is interpreted. Describing physical phenomena from graphs of a function and its derivative together, without algebra, is not developed.
No lesson shows that the gradient function of a^x is a constant multiple k a^x.
Calculator use appears (e^x key, ln and log keys). Using digital tools to tell rational from irrational values is not addressed.
log_a a = 1 and log_a 1 = 0 are used. log_a(1/x) = -log_a x is not justified.
The reflection in y = x is shown for a > 1. The case 0 < a < 1 is not shown.
Dilations are taught as y = af(x) and y = f(bx). The syllabus framing (replace x by x/k, y by y/l, factor k or l) is not used, so the factor-versus-coefficient link needs teaching.
No lesson treats replacing both x by x/k and y by y/k as an enlargement or reduction by factor k.
Tree diagrams appear as a multiplication-rule note and in practice questions. Arrays (two-dice grids) and tree diagrams for multistage events are not taught as their own method.
No lesson shows algebraically that P(A|B) = P(A) implies P(B|A) = P(B).
The product rule for independent events is stated and used. The proof in both directions from the conditional formula is not worked.

PD07 teaches histograms with frequency density plus box plots and stem-and-leaf plots (not 2024 Year 11). Relative and cumulative frequency histograms and polygons, and reading the mode and median from them, are not taught together.
